why: One of the two biggest Maths chapters. Derivative rules turn up everywhere, and tangents, maxima and minima give quick numericals.
The other giant chapter. Standard integrals, substitution and definite integrals are asked often and need fast, practised hands.
A large chapter: the discriminant, sum and product of roots, cube roots of unity and the factor theorem are quick to test and reused across algebra.
A big analytic geometry chapter full of short numericals: slopes, line equations, angles and distances from a point to a line.
Circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas give many formula-based questions on centres, foci, vertices, eccentricity and tangents.
Functions underpin limits, calculus and graphs. Domain, range, inverses and logarithm laws come up directly and inside other topics.
Vectors appear in both Maths and Physics. Dot and cross products, angles and areas make quick, reliable numericals.
A solid chapter where determinant properties and inverses can be tested quickly without long working, if the shortcuts are known.
Compound and double-angle identities are the engine of most trigonometry questions and are needed again in calculus.
Counting and probability questions are regular and short once nPr, nCr and the addition and multiplication rules are clear.
A.P. and G.P. formulas give fast questions on nth terms, sums and infinite series; a steady source of marks.
General term, middle term and binomial approximations are classic short questions with a fixed method.
Complex number operations, modulus and conjugate are quick to test and also feed the roots of quadratic equations.
Laws of sines and cosines, area formulas and the radii R and r give formula-driven triangle questions.
Standard limits and continuity checks are short questions, and limits are the base of differentiation.
Period, domain and range of trigonometric functions and maximum or minimum values are quick, recurring checks.
Order and degree, and separable first-order equations, form a short topic that extends integration directly.
Radians, arc length and signs of ratios in quadrants are fast to learn and needed in every later trigonometry chapter.
Sets, truth tables and group properties are mostly definitions; a quick win in the old Part I book.
Principal values and a few addition formulas cover most questions; small and quick to master.
General solutions of sin θ, cos θ and tan θ equations follow fixed patterns, so a little practice goes a long way.
A small chapter with one method; it also speeds up integration of rational functions.
Feasible regions and corner points are a short, visual topic; checking the corners usually gives the answer.
Newer-book topic: bisection, Newton–Raphson and the trapezium rule are fixed recipes that are quick to learn.
Velocity and acceleration as derivatives of displacement: one idea, quick to learn, and it overlaps with Physics.
A big chapter spanning Coulomb's law, fields, potential and capacitors; a favourite for numericals in ECAT preparation.
Equations of motion, Newton's laws, momentum and projectiles are core mechanics and give many quick numericals.
Resistance, power, EMF and Kirchhoff's rules give frequent circuit numericals that reward fast, clean working.
Gas laws, the first law, specific heats and Carnot efficiency form a broad chapter with formula-based questions.
v = fλ, beats, stationary waves and the Doppler effect give many short numericals and harmonic patterns.
Centripetal force, moment of inertia and orbital velocity are core mechanics with short numerical questions.
Magnetic forces on wires and charges, solenoids and galvanometer conversion give regular numericals.
Not the biggest chapter, but vector components, dot and cross products and torque are used throughout mechanics and electricity.
Work, energy, power and escape velocity give straightforward numericals once the formulas are fixed in memory.
Young's double slit, diffraction gratings and Malus's law are formula-based and give reliable optics questions.
Faraday's and Lenz's laws, motional EMF and transformers are tested both as concepts and as short numericals.
SHM equations, the spring and pendulum periods and energy in SHM are compact and often tested.
Dimensions, significant figures and error propagation are quick checks that also help verify answers in other chapters.
Rectification, transistors, op-amps and logic gates mix concepts and truth tables; logic gates are especially quick marks.
Photoelectric effect, de Broglie wavelength and Compton shift give short modern-physics numericals.
Half-life, binding energy and decay types give quick numericals and fact questions.
rms values, reactance, impedance and resonance frequency follow a few formulas that are easy to test.
Continuity and Bernoulli's equation, plus Stokes' law, are a short set of formulas that give quick marks.
Old-book chapter: magnifying power of microscopes and telescopes and optical fibres are formula and fact questions.
Young's modulus, stress and strain and types of magnetism are short and mostly definitions plus one formula.
Bohr energy levels and spectral series, X-rays and lasers form a compact chapter with a few key formulas.
Time dilation, length contraction and E = mc² are a few formulas that cover most questions.
Newer-book topic: quarks, leptons and the four fundamental forces are classification facts, quick to learn.
Newer-book topic: ultrasound, X-ray, CT and PET imaging are a handful of facts and principles.
Newer-book topic: Wien's law, Hubble's law and luminosity are short facts and simple relations.
The mole concept is the base of nearly every chemistry calculation; limiting reactant and yield problems are regular numericals.
The largest physical chemistry chapter: VSEPR shapes, hybridisation and bond order are asked often and explain much else.
Quantum numbers, electronic configurations and Bohr's model are core concepts with quick, rule-based questions.
Gas laws and pV = nRT give short numericals, and kinetic theory and ideal behaviour are favourite concept checks.
Kc, Kp and Le Chatelier's principle are tested as both concepts and numericals, and link to acids and industry.
pH, pOH, buffers and Ksp give regular numericals; acid-base concepts recur across inorganic and organic chemistry.
Oxidation numbers, electrode potentials and Faraday's laws are asked as both concepts and calculations.
Enthalpy definitions and Hess's law give clean numericals; sign conventions are a common trap worth practising.
Rate laws, order, half-life and activation energy are compact and often tested through short reasoning questions.
Functional groups, IUPAC names and isomerism are the gateway to every organic chapter that follows.
Alkane, alkene and alkyne reactions, Markovnikov's rule and ozonolysis are standard organic questions.
Trends in radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity are quick questions and explain the behaviour of every element group.
Intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonding and types of solids are a solid share of concept questions.
Molarity, molality and colligative properties give regular short calculations and concept checks.
Benzene's stability, electrophilic substitution and ortho-para versus meta directing groups are classic organic questions.
Alcohol classification, distinguishing tests and the acidity of phenol are regularly asked reaction questions.
Nucleophilic addition and the Tollens', Fehling's and iodoform tests are favourite questions for telling compounds apart.
Relative acidity of carboxylic acids and the reactions of their derivatives come up regularly in organic sections.
Variable oxidation states, colour, ligands and coordination numbers are concept questions with clear rules.
SN1, SN2 and elimination mechanisms and Grignard reagents link many organic conversions together.
Mostly descriptive facts on ammonia, nitric acid and sulphuric acid; learn the key reactions and conditions for quick marks.
Group 1 and 2 trends and the solubility and decomposition patterns are a short list of rules.
Halogen trends in oxidising power and HX stability are a few clear patterns, quick to revise.
Old-book chapter: borax, boric acid, silicones and lead compounds are a small set of facts.
Addition versus condensation polymers and the basic biomolecules are definitions and examples, fast to learn.
Separation methods and Rf values are short practical facts that are easy marks once read.
Newer-book topic: the basicity of amines and simple functional-group conversions build on earlier organic chapters.
Fertilisers, cement and Pakistan's chemical industries are a small set of facts worth quick revision.
Smog, acid rain, ozone depletion and water quality are general facts that are quick to learn.
Newer-book topic: a few IR and NMR ideas and the molecular ion peak cover most questions.
Old-book C chapters: if, switch, loops and functions are tested through output traces that need careful practice.
The new books' programming core: Python syntax, loops, lists and dictionaries are tested through short code-output questions.
A broad chapter in both old and new books: topologies, OSI and TCP/IP layers and devices give many definition questions.
Computer basics, memory types and number-system conversions are core facts; conversions are quick, sure marks.
Old-book C basics: data types, operator precedence and format specifiers are the base for every C trace question.
Old-book database chapters: keys, ER diagrams and normal forms are definition-heavy and regularly asked.
New-book topic: sorting, searching, stacks and queues are tested through short traces and definitions.
Old-book chapters on OS functions, word processing and spreadsheet formulas give quick fact and formula questions.
Malware, encryption, copyright and privacy appear in both old and new books and are mostly definitions.
Cloud service models, AI, IoT and blockchain (new books) plus computer applications (old book) are definition questions.
Old-book only: Access objects, field types and query kinds are a limited set of facts, quick to learn.
New-book topic: SDLC stages, Waterfall versus Agile and error types are short definitions with clear contrasts.
New-book topic: mean, median, mode and the basic data-science steps are short and quick to revise.
New-book topic: search techniques and design thinking are a few ideas, easy marks after one reading.
UET's English section is reading comprehension, so this unit is the whole English paper. Main idea, inference and words in context matter most.
Extra practice, not a separate ECAT section: a wider vocabulary makes words-in-context questions and every passage faster to read.
Extra practice, not a separate ECAT section: firm grammar helps you read passages precisely and spot options that change the meaning.
